title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a fabricated news article and interview impersonating real public figures, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler, to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The fake content was circulated online as a scam tool. This is a case of AI-enabled impersonation deployed entirely outside any legitimate use case, where the technology's ability to generate convincing false content was weaponized for fraud.

The system had no legitimate deployment context and no human authorization to create this content. Catching it would have required either preventing the AI from being used for impersonation in the first place through access controls, or having humans verify the authenticity of financial endorsements before they reached potential victims. ASIC reports that similar AI-generated investment scams featuring impersonated public figures are becoming increasingly common, with the broader category of scams it tracked increasing substantially year over year.

It is not established whether a single AI system was responsible for all such scams or how many different systems were involved in this growing trend.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake news article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler was circulated online, claiming they had a heated interview about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article and interview never actually occurred, representing a growing type of scam using artificial intelligence to create convincing but false content. ASIC reports that AI-generated investment scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent, with scammers building elaborate webs of deception including fake websites, news articles, reviews, and advertisements featuring impersonated celebrities and politicians.

Last year, ASIC took down 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase from the previous year, including 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated people. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through its public registers before investing, while Kohler argues that platforms hosting such content should face heavy fines.
